title: MH family risk and timing of prepared anesthesia
fairness: Review-wide scope: all 15 current proposed executable nodes were reviewed independently from their after/candidate visible fields; those fields match the current proposedCases. Prior PASS labels and author reasoning were not evidence of quality. The six Keep records, 69 retirement proposals, historical/parked attempts and held records are noted but not adjudicated. None of the 15 current cases has multiple nodes. No network or fresh source verification was used; editorial PASS is not clinical approval, and all drafts remain needs_clinician_review.

Proceed with the proposed nontriggering anesthetic and arrange specialist assessment is the best offered recommendation. Prior uneventful exposure and an uninformative panel do not negate the affected first-degree relative; that risk must then be separated from a requirement to finish definitive testing before prepared anesthesia.

The readiness details are decision-critical rather than an assertion that the patient is cleared. The three options have comparable length and address the same scheduling/preparation decision; no decisive nonmedical wording shortcut was found.

Self-contained: the anesthetic regimen, family testing context and preparation are present without a prior node. MH susceptibility and trigger avoidance are high-yield; this tests their application rather than drug-list recall.
suggestions: Preserve the distinction between maintaining MH precautions and completing susceptibility testing. Do not shorten the negative-panel description to a definitive negative familial test.
Clinical sign-off should confirm that the summarized facility readiness supports the intended setting; this offline review does not certify operational readiness or exact rescue provisions.

title: Seizure treatment during local-anesthetic toxicity with hypotension
clarityIssues: Minor tense friction: 'reviews ... after recovery' shifts to 'Generalized convulsions now continue.' The task makes the historical decision understandable, but a recorded-checkpoint transition would read more naturally.
fairness: Midazolam is the best offered agent for ongoing seizures in this toxicity context with persistent circulatory depression. Propofol and thiopental are real anticonvulsant/anesthetic alternatives whose hemodynamic effects matter; their use is not falsely described as universally prohibited.

Two consequential considerations remain: identify the toxic exposure pattern and select seizure suppression in the setting of hypotension. Ventilation, lipid therapy and circulatory support are already underway, so an omitted primary resuscitation action does not compete with the requested drug choice.
The three labels use identical grammar and specificity. Neither the drug name nor its class is supplied in the stem, and no nonmedical key cue was found.
The node is self-contained. Recognition and management of local-anesthetic systemic toxicity are high-yield; the hemodynamic constraint makes this more than naming its antidote.
suggestions: Optional clarity polish: introduce the last sentence with 'At the recorded treatment checkpoint' instead of 'now.'
Retain the explanation's qualification that midazolam still needs titration and respiratory support; do not convert the alternative-agent caution into an absolute.

title: Adjunct treatment for recurrent broad-complex rhythm during bupivacaine toxicity
clarityIssues: The prose repeats nearly all of the electrical exhibit. 'Reasonable' also sets a looser comparison than a single-best-answer task needs. Neither issue prevents solving this offered set.
fairness: Sodium bicarbonate is a defensible best adjunct among these three options for the represented local-anesthetic sodium-channel toxicity with broad complexes. The pulse, poor perfusion, already-delivered synchronized cardioversion and continuing resuscitation prevent the drug question from replacing urgent electrical treatment.

The uniform rhythm and absence of a rotating axis distinguish a torsades-oriented magnesium choice; lidocaine introduces another local anesthetic. These are medical discriminators, not word-matching cues for a reader without medical knowledge.

The inference combines toxicologic context with electrical findings and then selects an adjunct at the specified treatment stage. This is more specialized than the commonly tested initial LAST response, so the particular bicarbonate decision should not be represented as a core high-frequency general-surgery examination concept.

Uncertainty: the exact AHA recommendation strength and applicability were not independently source-verified in this offline review. No confident clinical inaccuracy is identified, but the explanation's limited-evidence qualifier must remain for clinician review.
Self-contained: seizure treatment, lipid administration and the recurrent rhythm are supplied locally. No preceding seizure-node answer is needed.
suggestions: Prefer 'Which additional medication is most appropriate ...' while preserving the explicit adjunctive treatment stage.
Let the exhibit carry the electrical observations and remove their duplicate prose. Retain the pulse, perfusion and treatment chronology.
Consider a lower-priority advanced item designation; retain core LAST coverage elsewhere.

title: Conflicting recovery assessments after rocuronium
clarityIssues: 'An eye muscle' is less precise than naming the monitored muscle, although the checked adductor-pollicis result is sufficient to resolve the offered decision.
fairness: Addressing residual rocuronium and reassessing is the best offered plan. The checked adductor-pollicis ratio conflicts with reassuring clinical strength and the eye-site result; the learner must decide which evidence establishes recovery and then act before extubation.

Fentanyl makes naloxone a recognizable competing drug, but opioid reversal does not correct the represented peripheral transmission deficit. Head lift and a reassuring eye-site ratio are credible extubation errors rather than arbitrary distractors.
No option is uniquely long or comprehensive. The extubation distractor repeats observations, but understanding why those observations are inadequate still requires medical knowledge.
Self-contained and high-yield: residual neuromuscular block and the limitations of clinical recovery tests are practical perioperative safety concepts.
suggestions: Name the monitored eye muscle if supported by the underlying record, without adding a pre-answer statement about which site is preferred.
Retain quantitative reassessment and the explanation's reminder that other extubation requirements still apply.

title: Timing and agent selection for cisatracurium reversal
clarityIssues: 'There is no immediate requirement to reverse paralysis' is an authored timing conclusion immediately before a task whose main remaining distinction is whether to reverse now or wait.

cues.phrase: There is no immediate requirement to reverse paralysis.
cues.why: Primes the only waiting option, 'Await further spontaneous recovery before neostigmine/glycopyrrolate,' against two immediate-drug alternatives. The preceding description already establishes ongoing anesthesia and ventilatory support.

fairness: Waiting for further spontaneous recovery before relying on neostigmine is defensible as the best offered plan; sugammadex is not the reversal agent for cisatracurium. Drug identity and measured block depth provide two clinically consequential decisions.

The explanation appropriately describes unreliable reversal at the represented depth rather than an absolute prohibition. Giving neostigmine now and continuing support is not intrinsically impossible; the item should teach comparative reliability, not declare that approach universally incorrect.
Self-contained and high-yield. No missing earlier result is needed. The difficulty is moderate because the drug-class and depth distinction survives removal of the timing hint.
suggestions: Delete the sentence announcing no immediate reversal requirement. Retain the actual airway, anesthesia, ventilation and quantitative-monitoring facts that make waiting safe.

Have clinical sign-off confirm the comparative timing recommendation at the stated depth. Keep the explanation qualified and do not invent a waiting interval or imply that simply obtaining four twitches guarantees adequate recovery.

title: Normalized acceleromyography and reversal in severe renal impairment
fairness: The stated raw measurement and baseline give a normalized ratio of 1.02/1.20 = 0.85. The device behavior is explicit, so the learner need not guess whether normalization or capping was already performed.

Neostigmine/glycopyrrolate with quantitative reassessment is the best offered plan: residual block remains, while severe renal impairment makes routine sugammadex selection less appropriate. This combines monitor interpretation with a patient-specific reversal choice; both change the action.
The options are concrete and comparably scoped. Clinical strength competes credibly with the monitor evidence, and the renal condition does not identify an answer without pharmacologic knowledge.
The explanation says sugammadex is 'not recommended,' not absolutely impossible in every circumstance. No new renal cutoff or dosing rule is needed to solve the offered set.
Self-contained. Residual-block prevention and reversal selection are high-yield; baseline normalization is a legitimate advanced technical discriminator rather than ambiguity.
suggestions: Preserve the explicit raw-display and baseline information and the worked normalization in feedback.
Keep clinical sign-off focused on the exact monitoring method and renal-context antagonist ranking; do not generalize the key to every device or every degree of renal dysfunction.

title: Recurrent respiratory depression after naloxone response
clarityIssues: 'Checked quantitative hand response returned to baseline' is less precise than naming the measured transmission quantity. The explanation also says motor recovery 'remains documented,' whereas the presentation explicitly gives an earlier recovery measurement, not a repeat assessment at recurrence.

cues.why: Names the successful drug immediately before the same problem recurs. 'Repeat titrated naloxone' can be selected by repeat-what-worked reasoning without distinguishing the three drug mechanisms.

fairness: Repeat titrated naloxone during respiratory support is clinically defensible and best supported by the recorded response. Mixed drug effects remain possible; the explanation correctly avoids claiming an exclusive opioid cause.

The prior response supplies most of the target inference, and the block-recovery statement weakens the sugammadex distractor. The remaining act is repetition of the named successful treatment, not two consequential resident-level steps.
The case stands alone. The concept is high-yield, but the present construction is a basic recurrence-recognition item, without an explicit accepted basic role.
suggestions: Either seek an explicit basic safety/recognition designation or replace this scored objective with a distinct decision whose answer changes with a current reassessment. Do not merely hide a clinically necessary treatment response.
Avoid duplicating the more consequential delivery-plan node. If retained, specify the actual quantitative measurement and keep the explanation's chronology no stronger than the observations supplied.

title: Naloxone delivery after repeated respiratory relapses

cues.phrase: IV access, infusion equipment and continuous bedside monitoring are available.
cues.why: Minor priming: 'infusion equipment' repeats the key's delivery method. It does not establish that an infusion is preferable to usable IV boluses; that ranking still depends on the repeated unsupported-breathing gaps.

fairness: A respiratory-response-adjusted IV infusion is the best offered maintenance strategy given repeated return of hypoventilation requiring assisted ventilation between effective rescues. IV boluses remain clinically useful, so the explanation correctly favors rather than universally mandates infusion.

Two steps are consequential: use repeated reversal responses to identify an ongoing reversible opioid component, then use the relapse trajectory to choose sustained titratable delivery. Pain and respiratory support remain relevant to the treatment target.

The options are parallel delivery plans. IM dosing is less attractive with IV access and a need for close titration, but the credible IV-bolus alternative prevents the equipment sentence from resolving the question by itself.

Self-contained and coherent with the separate recurrence and endpoint vignettes. High-yield postoperative respiratory-depression management; no invented recurrence count or time threshold is asserted.
suggestions: Trim the equipment inventory if the monitored hospital setting already establishes the offered treatments' feasibility. Retain the relapse/support trajectory.
If these separate cases are ever recombined, review the first node's feedback against this task; do not place an infusion recommendation in earlier feedback.

title: Early naloxone-infusion endpoint with residual dozing
fairness: Maintaining the present rate is the best offered immediate adjustment: spontaneous ventilation and responsiveness have improved, pain is tolerable, and this is only the first early reassessment after repeated relapses.

The resident must distinguish an adequate respiratory endpoint from complete wakefulness, then decide whether the recent relapse history permits stopping treatment. Increasing for dozing and stopping after an initial success are different credible errors.
The task clearly asks for an immediate infusion adjustment, not discharge eligibility or a later weaning plan. The options are parallel and there is no unique wording match or length cue.
Self-contained: the repeated rescues and current response are restated without requiring the delivery-plan node. This is high-yield opioid-reversal titration and monitoring.
suggestions: Preserve both the current respiratory observations and the early timing relative to recurrent hypoventilation; removing either would weaken the ranking.
If recombined with the delivery-plan case, keep the prior explanation from prescribing this exact maintenance decision. Do not add an unsupported fixed observation or infusion duration.

title: Route-specific midazolam planning with cobicistat
clarityIssues: 'That earlier record documents the increments and responses' adds little because the actual increments and responses are not displayed and no calculation uses them.
fairness: Omitting oral midazolam and starting with smaller IV increments is the best offered revision. The learner must recognize the newly relevant interaction, then apply its different implications to oral exposure and monitored repeated IV administration.

The four combinations balance both component frequencies, so convergence cannot reconstruct the key. The common IV monitoring/titration conditions apply to every IV plan rather than making only the key safe by wording.

The prior dosing record predates cobicistat, providing a real reason not to simply reuse it. No exact dose reduction is invented; the explanation retains the need for individualized titration and the qualification that reduction is considered especially with repeated use.

Self-contained. Perioperative drug interactions and altered sedative exposure are high-yield, although the precise boosted-antiretroviral route distinction is more specialized than basic benzodiazepine reversal.
suggestions: Delete the unused sentence announcing the earlier record's increments and responses; retain that the copied IV increments predate cobicistat.
Keep all IV options under the same monitoring conditions and retain balanced paired components. Do not imply that every form of midazolam is categorically contraindicated.

title: Response to gradual CO2 rise during insufflation

cues.why: Repeats the modifiable variable named only in the key, 'Increase minute ventilation and reassess.' This provides a weak nonmedical unchanged-variable-to-change-variable shortcut, strengthened by the absence of any competing ventilation plan.

fairness: Increasing minute ventilation and reassessing is the best offered initial response to the represented gradual rise after insufflation. A zero inspired CO2 baseline makes absorber failure less likely; stable accompanying observations make immediate dantrolene less supported.
Stable temperature alone would not exclude early MH. The explanation does not make that absolute claim and appropriately allows another cause to emerge; preserve that distinction.

The alternative mechanisms are largely removed by dedicated observations. The remaining task is the familiar increased-CO2-load to increased-ventilation association, not two consequential steps with a close management competitor.
Self-contained and high-yield, but easy for the intended resident audience.
suggestions: Retain the safety information, but add a genuinely decision-changing response trajectory or supported ventilatory constraint and compare realistic same-stage responses. Do not manufacture difficulty by omitting the inspired baseline or hiding signs of deterioration.
Alternatively request explicit acceptance as basic laparoscopic physiology rather than classifying this version as a difficult two-step item.

title: Hemodynamic and airway-pressure changes after insufflation increase
clarityIssues: The table offers only qualitative 'Higher' changes in peak and plateau pressure. It supports an elastic-load contribution, but does not establish that the resistive component is unchanged; the explanation should not be read as excluding mixed physiology.
The exhibit caption's 'no post-intervention findings are shown' is review-process language rather than useful clinical information.

cues.phrase: the surgeon has just increased insufflation pressure
cues.why: Names the single changed exposure immediately before deterioration; only the key reverses that exact change. A reader can choose it without interpreting ventricular filling, ejection fraction or airway mechanics.

cues.phrase: No pressure-reduction trial has yet been performed.
cues.why: Announces the missing action that appears in the key, 'Lower insufflation pressure and reassess.' This is the named-omission cue prohibited by the authoring standard.

fairness: Lowering insufflation pressure and reassessing is a reasonable best next action with this temporal relationship and deteriorating perfusion. No confident clinical error is identified in that key.

The detailed table fails the consequential-data deletion test: the same immediate correction follows from the isolated pressure increase and deterioration without reading the table. Bronchodilator and inotropic support are weak competitors against reversing the sole newly changed exposure.

Self-contained. The cardiovascular and respiratory effects of pneumoperitoneum are high-yield, but this version measures obvious reversal of a preceding change rather than the intended integrated physiological reasoning.
suggestions: Remove the named-omission sentence and review-process caption wording.
Redesign the decision so a supported physiological observation changes the ranking of realistic next actions; merely adding more echo or pressure data will not fix the current shortcut.

If a peak-minus-plateau comparison is intended to decide treatment, provide adequate supported observations for that comparison. Do not infer identical changes from two entries that merely say 'Higher.'

title: Confirmatory measurement for post-benzocaine saturation discrepancy

cues.why: Co-oximetry is the only new measurement class; 'Repeat arterial gas' and 'Second-site two-wavelength pulse oximetry' repeat methods already described. Novelty can favor the key without interpreting the saturation discrepancy.

fairness: Co-oximetry is the best offered measurement. Benzocaine exposure, persistent cyanosis/low pulse oximetry and preserved arterial oxygen tension with calculated saturation coherently support investigating dyshemoglobinemia.
The accurate feedback distinguishes calculated saturation from measured hemoglobin fractions. No confident clinical inaccuracy is identified.

The stem gives the classic diagnostic association, and both distractors largely repeat completed methods. Naming the suspected problem and its standard confirmatory test is one recall chain here, not two consequential decisions.
Self-contained and high-yield. The subsequent hemolysis vignette is separately supplied and is not needed to answer this node.
suggestions: Replace the novelty cue and repeated-test foils with comparably credible measurement/report-interpretation alternatives, using a real adequacy or method distinction that changes the decision.
Alternatively seek explicit basic recognition acceptance. Preserve the calculated-versus-measured distinction rather than making the case artificially difficult by withholding it.

title: Symptomatic hemolytic anemia after methylene blue
fairness: Packed red-cell transfusion is the best offered treatment for the represented marked symptomatic anemia with current methemoglobin within reference. Ascorbic acid does not replace lost oxygen-carrying capacity, and red-cell exchange is not supported by the resolved dyshemoglobinemia in this record.

No decisive nonmedical wording shortcut was found. The weakness is clinical ease: hemoglobin 5.6 g/dL with dyspnea, tachycardia and pallor already selects transfusion, while current normal methemoglobin removes the reason to consider the other two options.

The detailed hemolysis/G6PD findings do not change the scored treatment. The presentation has also already withheld further methylene blue, so the meaningful drug-safety decision is completed before the learner acts.
The low G6PD result supports the safety concern; the item does not use a normal acute-hemolysis assay to exclude deficiency. No confident clinical inaccuracy is identified.

Self-contained: exposure, treatment, current reassessment and changed problem are all supplied. Hemolysis, G6PD-related drug toxicity and treatment of symptomatic anemia are high-yield, but this version is a straightforward anemia rescue item rather than a difficult pharmacology decision.
suggestions: Either accept this explicitly as basic safety recognition or redesign the scored decision so the current hemoglobin-fraction findings and treatment history are both necessary to choose among credible actions.
Do not obscure the severe anemia or withhold current methemoglobin to manufacture difficulty. Remove unused diagnostic detail if the objective remains transfusion for symptomatic anemia.
If returned to a multi-part case, avoid teaching the exact later treatment in the earlier confirmation feedback.

title: Anticipated difficult intubation and ventilation

cues.why: Both distractors begin with the identical sequence, leaving 'Secure the trachea awake before inducing general anesthesia' as the structural outlier. This is a weak key-only contrast cue rather than a decisive proof; the dominant weakness remains the straightforward clinical recognition task.

fairness: Awake tracheal securing is the best offered strategy given prior difficult intubation, difficult mask ventilation, persistent anatomical limitations and cooperation. The question does not assert that a particular device or sedation regimen is mandatory.

The history already states difficulty with both intubation and rescue ventilation. Both alternatives induce anesthesia before securing the airway, so the same familiar difficult-airway rule dismisses both; there is no second independently consequential decision in this option set.
Self-contained and coherent. Difficult-airway planning is high-yield, but multiple risk descriptors do not by themselves make the question hard or two-step.
suggestions: Seek explicit acceptance as a basic airway-safety item, or introduce a supported patient-specific planning decision among genuinely credible strategies whose ranking depends on more than recognizing the named difficult-airway history.
Do not add unsafe induction options merely to increase option count, and do not force a specific awake device without the anatomical and procedural information needed to distinguish it.
